photo.fileTitle: File:Glass phial of British Standard penicillin, London, England, Wellcome L0059573.jpg
photo.caption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin
photo.alt: The tag on the vial says: "Medical Research Council - British Standard Penicillin - Contensts = Approximately 30 mg - 1 mg = 1600 standard units of penicillin" and dated 27 April 1946
photo.description: British Standard penicillin was defined as one milligram of penicillin containing 1,600 International Units. An International Unit is defined as the potency or activity of a drug. The standard was set by the National Institute for Medical Research. International Standards were set in 1944 and in 1952. Standardisation of drugs such as penicillin is important to ensure the quantity and quality produced and given to patients is consistent all over the world. maker: National Institute for Medical Research Place made: London, Greater London, England

rights.fileTitle: File:Penicillin fermentation vessel, England Wellcome L0059171.jpg

photo.fileTitle: File:Penicillin fermentation vessel, England Wellcome L0059171.jpg
photo.caption: Thousands of glass fermentation vessels like this one were used in laboratories to produce penicillin. The mould was grown on the surface of a liquid filled with nutrients. The stopper kept contaminants out while allowing the mould to get fresh air.
photo.alt: A sealed glass cyclider with a spout. There is dark liquid at the bottom and a brown substance on which mould is growing. The spout has a cotton wool stopper.
photo.description: Penicillin fermentation vessel, England, 1940-1945 Thousands of glass fermentation vessels like this one were used in Glaxo (now GlaxoSmithKline) laboratories to produce penicillin. The penicillium mould was grown on the surface of a liquid filled with all the nutrients it needed. This approach was superseded by the method of growing the mould within large industrial fermenters. The antibiotic was first used in the early 1940s and saved the lives of many soldiers during the Second World War. Medical Photographic Library Penicillin fermentation

photo.caption: Mould being strained at the harvest table during the manufacture of penicillin at the Commonwealth Serum Laboratories in Parkville, Victoria.
photo.alt: Technicians tip the contents of mould flasks into troughs with a gauze cover. Here the bottles are not cylindrical but flat oblongs with rounded edges and the spout is in the middle of one of the short sides, more like a conventional flat bottle.

photo.caption: Antibiotic resistance is a growing public health concern.
photo.alt: A poster expleing antiobiotc resistance "from farm to table". The poster explains that feeding antibiotics to animals evolves resistant bacteria; this spreads to our food and environment; which then gets into our food and makes us sick
photo.description: All animals carry bacteria in their intestines. Antibiotics are given to animals. Antibiotics kill most bacteria. But resistant bacteria survive and multiply.

rights.fileTitle: File:Antibiotic use in livestock, OWID.svg

photo.caption: Antibiotic use in livestock
photo.alt: World political map shaded with colours showing the milligrams of total antibiotic use per kilogram of meat production. Highest use is in Belgium, Germany, Italy, Spain and Hungary; Canada, Saudi Arabia, Japan and Malaysia come next; then the United
photo.description: :Antibiotic use in livestock Antibiotics are used in livestock for animal health and productivity, but also pose a risk for antibiotic resistance in both humans and livestock. Data is measured as the milligrams of total antibiotic use per kilogram of meat production. This is corrected for differences in livestock numbers and types, normalising to a population-corrected unit (PCU).
